extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and structuring plot in short stories and novels, focusing on the major dramatic question, protagonist/goal/conflict dynamics, and the roles of beginning, middle, and end (including subplots and novel-scale differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Major dramatic question
rubrics_metrics.description: A single question that the story pursues—usually answerable with a yes, no, or maybe—which arises from the relationship among three elements: the protagonist, his or her goal, and the conflict blocking that goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This question should be established early and stay central to the plot; examples: 'Will Holden find a place where he belongs?' The story's events should drive toward answering this specific question, not some other question that happens to arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The main character—the most complex, dimensional, and closely followed character in the piece; the major dramatic question always centers around this character and what will happen in his or her life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically there is one protagonist (though novels can have multiple); because the reader is taken deep into this character, the protagonist must be fully illuminated and believable (examples: Holden Caulfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist's goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The desire at the heart of the protagonist that drives the story; the goal is what the protagonist wants most and is tied to getting a yes/no answer to the major dramatic question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals can be conscious or unconscious, concrete or abstract. Abstract goals generally need a concrete representation in the story (e.g., abstract desire for belonging represented by going to New York to find someone who understands). The goal should push the question into view for the reader and shape the plot's events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict (obstacles and escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obstacles—external and/or internal—that block the protagonist's goal create conflict, and plot depends on conflict; conflict should escalate across the piece until one side gives out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External obstacles include antagonists, society, nature, physical limits; internal obstacles include fears, inadequacies, or lack of knowledge. Stories with real depth generally require at least some internal conflict. List many obstacles in planning; the more fierce and escalating the fight, the more interesting the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginning: start/time & exposition & question
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning must (1) drop the reader into the middle of the action (start at the point of change), (2) provide the necessary background exposition on a need-to-know basis, and (3) establish the major dramatic question as close to the beginning as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not begin when 'nothing's happening'; avoid too much background up front—supply only what's needed for the moment and integrate exposition with action. Example: 'The first job of a story's beginning is to start at the right time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle: chain of events and rising tension
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle (usually the vast majority of the work) is where the protagonist repeatedly encounters increasingly daunting obstacles; events should form a tight chain of cause-and-effect that builds tension toward a crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid random or arbitrarily ordered events—plot requires causal linkage (Forster example: 'The Queen died and then the King died of grief'). The middle must tighten links between events so tension rises steadily until it can increase no further.

rubrics_metrics.name: End: crisis, climax, and consequences (the three C's)
rubrics_metrics.description: The end (often shortest) should contain crisis (tension maximum), climax (the breaking of tension and the answer to the major dramatic question), and consequences (the aftermath), collectively resolving the pursued question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences in contemporary fiction are often implied rather than spelled out—readers feel them more than they are narrated. An ending should feel 'inevitable but unexpected'—looking back it makes sense, yet it is striking when it happens (examples: 'Cathedral' climax; comparison to Dickens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause-and-effect unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the fictional universe must be causally linked—characters' actions should produce believable reactions and consequences so that the plot forms a coherent chain rather than a pile of unrelated incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize causal relationships when plotting; each event should follow logically from prior events or character choices, thereby contributing to rising tension and the plot's overall arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot: relevance and function
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot is a plotline running alongside the main plot that must be relevant to and comment on the main plot; it can focus on another character or a related issue and may serve as parallel or contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In novels subplots are possible because of length; they can produce multiple climaxes and echoes of the main plot (parallel or contrasting fates). Subplots are optional—tight, focused works may omit them to preserve intensity (e.g., The Catcher in the Rye).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying structure to novels (proportions & possibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning/middle/end functions remain the same in novels as in short stories, but proportions change: the middle occupies a much larger share, beginnings may be longer (more upfront exposition integrated with action), and endings can allow consequences to play out more fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the novel's extra room deliberately—develop characters, raise and intensify obstacles, and consider whether to include subplots or multiple climaxes. Even with more pages, each page should advance the linked chain of events toward the climactic answer.
